activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Clara taped the photocopy inside her locker door so she would see it every morning: six columns for six days, the seventh left blank and titled, in her handwriting, REST. She had not written anything in the other columns yet. It was Wednesday, and Ms. Popal wanted the training program by Friday, one full week for a runner of her own choosing, with warm-ups scheduled in ink.

The problem was that she had chosen herself, and she did not trust the blank column.

She had run every day since September. Ten kilometres on Monday, intervals on Tuesday, hills on Wednesday, and so on through Sunday, which she treated as a slower reward lap rather than a day off, because a day off felt like a day of losing. By October her times had gone the wrong way. At the meet on Saturday she had been eleven seconds slower than the week before, and Eden, waiting at the fence with both hands around a paper cup of tea, had not said anything cruel, which was somehow worse.

"You looked like a person carrying furniture," Eden said finally.

"I felt like one."

They were sitting on the low wall behind the gym, the parking lot emptying behind them. Clara pulled her notebook out of her bag and showed Eden the empty grid, the blank column, the word REST sitting there like an accusation. Eden squinted at it.

"My brother does weights," Eden said. "He calls it supercompensation."

"Calls what supercompensation."

"The rest days. The idea that you get fitter in recovery, after the workout, when the body rebuilds past where it was. Not during the workout itself."

Clara looked at her own knees, at the taping on her left one, at the grass going brown along the edge of the wall. She thought of all those mornings she had malign as lazy the girls who took Thursdays off, the ones she privately called revisionist about training, rewriting hard work into something gentle and pleasant, and she felt her face warm. She had been the one rewriting things, only her version was the harsh one, the one that said the workout itself made you faster, which apparently it did not.

"I've been doing it backwards," she said.

"You've been doing it forwards. Just all of it forwards."

On Thursday Clara sat in the library during her free period with the grid in front of her and a pencil she kept flipping. Noam, at the next table, leaned over and read her column headers upside down, which she hated. "Why is Monday nothing?" he asked. Monday was the blank one now; she had moved it from Sunday, still unsure which day the body would want, still unsure how a person was supposed to know that.

"It's rest," she said. "You get fitter in the recovery, not the session."

"Then why does everyone train all the time?"

She didn't have an answer, so she sharpened her pencil longer than it needed.

In class on Friday, Ms. Popal went desk to desk collecting the programs, pausing at Clara's long enough that Clara stopped breathing. Warm-up, fifteen minutes, listed before every session. Hard intervals on Tuesday, easy kilometres on Wednesday, hills Friday, and Monday a box with nothing in it except one word. Ms. Popal circled the word and wrote a small check beside it, and moved on without comment. Clara watched her go and felt let down by the silence, then embarrassed at needing praise for the thing itself.

That night she told her mother she was not going to the track, and her mother said, carefully, "Are you feeling disaffected with it?" as if Clara had joined some quiet rebellion against her own sport. Clara said no. She said she was trying to get faster, which was the opposite.

Sunday, two weeks into the program, Eden came to the wall after Clara's easy run and held the stopwatch while Clara jogged the warm-up loops, then ran one timed kilometre, just to see. Clara came through the line and bent over, hands on knees, and Eden looked at the watch and then at Clara and did not say anything for a second.

"Tell me."

"Three seconds faster than your meet time. Off one kilometre. On a Sunday."

Clara straightened up. She wanted to say that one kilometre proved nothing, that a week was nothing, that she might just have slept well or eaten well or caught a tailwind, and all of that was true and none of it changed the grid folded in her pocket with its blank, usefully blank, Monday. She held out her hand for the watch.

"Again," she said.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: In Westminster-style parliaments such as the UK's, the second reading is a debate and vote on a bill's general principles, before its details are examined.
story:
The motion on the order paper read: "Second Reading of the School Transit Fairness Bill." Alexa had spent two evenings reading the UK parliament's website for Ms. Warsame's civics assignment, and one phrase kept returning to her: second readings were debates on principles, not details. She had underlined it twice, then felt embarrassed at her own thoroughness, as though she were rehearsing a part in a play everyone else had decided to improvise.

The classroom had been rearranged into a horseshoe of desks, each with a folded paper nameplate. Eleanor wanted to be Speaker and had asked for it with the particular brightness she reserved for roles involving a gavel, which here was a whiteboard eraser. Jazmine, voluble even at nine in the morning, had drafted the bill herself, all six clauses of it, and had printed copies that she now distributed like a dealer laying out cards.

"Second reading," Eleanor announced, rapping the eraser, "is a debate and vote on the bill's general principles. Details come after." Alexa felt a small, unreasonable gladness that someone else had read the same page.

The bill proposed that discounted bus passes be extended to students who lived just outside the district boundary, a category that included Alexa herself and, more urgently, included the kids from the farm roads east of town who paid full fare or walked. Jazmine opened with force: access to school was access to education, and a boundary line drawn for tax purposes should not disenfranchise students who happened to live on the wrong side of a field. Alexa found herself nodding before she had decided to.

Then a boy near the window, one of the government benches, stood holding his copy of the bill at arm's length like a specimen. "Clause three, line two," he said. "There's a comma after 'eligible students' where there should be a semicolon. As drafted, it could be read to include recent graduates."

A pause. Then someone else stood to argue that the comma was correct. Then someone produced a red pen and began marking his copy aloud. Within a minute the chamber had collapsed into punctuation, three people talking at once about restrictive and non-restrictive clauses, and Jazmine leaning over her draft saying that grammar was not the point, and the boy with the red pen saying that drafting was exactly the point, that sloppy bills made sloppy laws.

Alexa stood. She had not planned to; her knees did it first and her voice followed. "What's the point of the second reading?" she asked, and the room actually went quiet, which surprised her more than standing had.

"Debate the principles," Eleanor said, from the Speaker's chair, in the tone of someone reminding the class what page they were on.

"Right. Principles before details." Alexa heard her own voice steadier than she felt. "Whether students who live outside the boundary deserve the same fare as everyone else, that's the principle. The comma is a detail. It gets examined after, clause by clause." She looked at the boy with the red pen. "You're not wrong that it matters. You're just wrong about when it matters."

The boy sat down slowly, the way people do when they are deciding whether they have been defeated or merely postponed. Someone on the government side stood and said the principle was sound but the money was the problem, that the board's transport budget was fixed and the discount would have to come from somewhere. Jazmine countered that the somewhere could be the surplus from last year's pass sales, a figure she produced from her notebook with the flourish of a magician revealing a dove. Alexa listened and found she believed both of them, or believed each of them in turn, which was not the same thing and might be more honest.

They voted on the general principles, a show of hands along the horseshoe, and it carried, nineteen to eleven. Eleanor declared the bill had passed second reading and would proceed to committee, where, she added, the comma could expect a full hearing. A laugh went around the room at the boy's expense, and he grinned and raised his red pen in mock triumph, and Alexa found she liked him better for it.

Afterward, while the desks were being pushed back into rows, Jazmine asked Alexa whether she thought the bill would survive committee, whether the fare thing could actually happen or whether it was all, in the end, an exercise. "I don't know," Alexa said, stacking the printed copies. "The debate was real. The vote was real. Whether real votes about real commas become real passes, that part we haven't done yet." Jazmine took the copies back, squared their edges, and slid them into her binder with the care of someone saving evidence.

Ms. Warsame, who had said almost nothing all period, wrote one line on the whiteboard before the bell: Third Reading, Thursday. Then she capped the marker and left it on the ledge.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration is C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy: glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water.
story:
The smell of the clinic was antiseptic underneath and dog on top, and Logan stood at the reception desk holding a biology textbook he had not opened since September. He was there because Ms. Watanabe, the veterinarian who lived two houses down from his aunt, had agreed to let him shadow on Saturday mornings, and because his biology mark was low enough that his teacher had offered a deal: show me you understand cellular respiration, and I will exonerate the missing lab reports from your average. Logan had said yes before he understood what he was signing up for, which was, so far, standing around while other people did interesting things.

"Scale," Ms. Watanabe said, and a technician lifted a trembling terrier onto it. "Six point two kilos. Write it on the board, please." She pointed to the whiteboard by the exam room door, where the day's patients went in a column, and Logan wrote the numbers. He had assumed he would watch surgery, or at least a vaccination. Instead he was the board boy, the runner of charts, and his textbook sat on the counter like an accusation.

Romain arrived at eleven with his dog, a mutt named after a cereal, for a follow-up on a cut paw. Romain was in Logan's biology class, and when he spotted the textbook his face went through something tectonic, a whole continent of amusement shifting at once. "You're studying here? Voluntarily?"

"Make-up assignment," Logan said. "Cellular respiration. I have to trace it from glucose to ATP, in the mitochondria, and I don't get it, and if I fail it my mark stays dead."

Romain sat on the bench with the dog across his knees. "You could just memorize the equation."

"I can memorize anything. That's not the same as getting it." Logan heard how pompous that sounded only after it was out, but Romain didn't laugh, which surprised him.

Before anything else could happen, the door opened and Jaxon came in fast, carrying a shoebox with holes punched in the lid. Inside was a sparrow, adult, wing at a wrong angle, found on the sidewalk outside the rink where Jaxon had been shooting pucks since seven. Ms. Watanabe took the box without a word about hockey or Saturdays, cupped the bird in one hand, and held a small mirror to its beak. The mirror fogged, faintly, in pulses.

"She's breathing," Logan said, before he thought about whether it was a useful thing to say.

"She is. Watch the fog. Every breath out carries carbon dioxide and water, and that's the end of a very long story." She set the bird in an incubator with warmed oxygen flowing in through a thin tube. "She's cold and shocky. I'm going to give her glucose, sugar, because her body's run out of fuel to burn."

Logan looked at the textbook on the counter. Something nudged at him. "Glucose," he said. "And the oxygen you're giving her. That's the equation, isn't it? Glucose plus oxygen becomes carbon dioxide plus water, plus energy." He went to the whiteboard, wiped the patient column to one side with his sleeve, and wrote C6H12O6 + 6 O2, then an arrow, then 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy.

"Six of each," Romain said from the bench, leaning to see. "You forgot the sixes, you put them on the water but not the oxygen." He was right; the oxygen had been bare. Logan added the coefficients, and Romain came over and checked each number against the page in the book like an auditor, because Romain was the kind of person who kept his lineage of small correctnesses unbroken.

"So the fog on the mirror," Logan said slowly, "is the water from the equation. And the carbon in the carbon dioxide, that came out of the glucose." He looked at the sparrow, tiny and intent on staying alive inside the plastic box. "The sugar Ms. Watanabe gave her, and the oxygen going in through the tube, they're meeting in her cells. In the mitochondria. And what comes out is the fog and the energy she needs to keep breathing."

"That's the whole of it," Ms. Watanabe said, not looking up from adjusting the oxygen flow. "Now you know why I give sugar and not protein."

Jaxon had drifted toward the incubator, pucks forgotten. "Can I stay until she's warm?" he asked, and Ms. Watanabe glanced at the clock, then at the boy's face, and said he could sit in the corner chair as long as he was quiet. Romain's dog, sensing an audience, put its bandaged paw delicately on Romain's knee, and Romain said, "Yes, you too, you're all patients today."

Logan copied the equation onto a clean page of his notebook. He understood the arithmetic now, the way six oxygens and six carbons had to come from somewhere and go somewhere, but there was still a stretch of it he could not see, the part inside the mitochondria where the energy was actually caught and passed along, and his teacher would want that too, traced step by step. He would have to go back to the chapter and work at it. He looked at the sparrow breathing her small fogged breaths, and at Jaxon watching her, and he left the equation on the whiteboard with the patient list, so it would still be there next Saturday.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.
story:
The rink smelled the way it always did in November, of cold rubber and burnt sugar from the vending machine, and Evan sat lacing his skates in the third stall from the door because the laces there were still whole. Across the room Jacoby was taping his stick with the small, ferocious care he gave everything, though they were a week from the first game and nobody had yet told them who would wear the assistant captain's letter. Jacoby wanted it the way some people want weather, personally, as though the coaches were withholding something owed to him.

Mr. Harper, who ran the rink and had run it since Evan's father played here, came out of the office with a laminated sheet in one hand and a look of official reluctance. He pinned it to the corkboard by the skate racks and tapped it twice. "New warm-up," he said. "Before any of you touches the ice. Landings, cuts, balance work. Ten minutes. Complaints go to the league, not to me."

The complaints metastasized anyway, moving from stall to stall in low voices until by the second week they had reached every corner of the room. Jacoby said it was ballet for people who couldn't skate. A defenseman named only by his number said his older brother had never done a single hopping drill in six seasons. Evan said nothing, mostly because he had twisted his knee in tryouts the year before, quietly, in a boring drill, and had spent four weeks watching his season shrink to nothing while the boreal dark came down over the parking lot at four in the afternoon.

He was the one who finally went to the corkboard, partly to be moving, partly because Kathleen had asked him what the sheet actually said and he did not know. Kathleen had joined the team's off-ice training group to build her college application file and stayed, she claimed, for the vending machine, and she read over his shoulder with the patience of someone who read everything twice. The sheet was dense, league-issued, full of small print about neuromuscular warm-up programs, and one sentence sat at the bottom in bold: programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique had been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries.

"Neuromuscular," Kathleen said slowly. "So it's the muscles talking to the nerves. Or the other way around."

"I think the point is the talking," Evan said.

He read the sentence again while Jacoby slapped pucks against the boards behind them, and he found he could not dismiss it, though he wanted to, because wanting to was easier than admitting that the boring thing might be the real thing. His father, who fixed transmissions for a living, trusted only what he could put his hands on, and had taught Evan that anything printed in bold by a committee was probably a way of selling something. But Evan had also watched his knee fail in a slow, ordinary motion, and the bold sentence described a program for exactly that, in exactly the language of exactly that failure.

The next morning, before the others arrived, he did the whole sequence alone at the far end of the rink, landing off the small plywood box Mr. Harper had built, cutting around cones, wobbling, correcting. It was tedious in a way that felt almost private, like practicing handwriting. Mr. Harper came out with the zam and watched him finish one landing drill before he flooded the ice, and said only, "Box stays by the door," which was the closest he came to praise.

At Thursday's practice Jacoby led the grumbling again, louder now, because the letter had gone to a senior and Jacoby's season had a dent in it that he carried like a stone in a pocket. Evan waited until the drills were assigned, then skated over to the box and dragged it onto the ice. He told the defensemen what he had read, one sentence, plainly, and said he'd messed up a knee doing nothing harder than a crossover and did not intend to do it again. Jacoby circled at the blue line, jaw working, plainly deciding whether this was betrayal or a kind of argument.

He came over eventually, set a foot on the box, and looked at Evan with the flat attention he gave opponents. "Fine," he said. "Show me the landing one. And if you laugh, I'm putting you into the boards." Kathleen, already in line behind them, called out that she had no such promise from anyone, and the boreal dark pressed against the rink windows, and Evan dropped his weight onto the box, sprang, and landed soft, both knees bent, waiting for Jacoby to do the same.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
Elizabeth had agreed to volunteer at the community kitchen every Saturday for a month, mostly because Kassidy had signed them up together and it seemed cowardly to back out after Kassidy's grandmother died. She had not expected the chocolate. Behind the racks of donated bread there was a pallet of couverture, dark and milk, left over from a bakery that closed in the spring, and Ms. Robinson, who ran the kitchen, had said that if anyone could learn to temper it, the truffles could go into the holiday boxes for families on the mailing list.

She printed a page from the library computer and read it on the bus: melt, cool, reheat slightly, test on the back of a spoon. The chocolate should set shiny and snap when you broke it. That was the whole discipline, apparently, a matter of holding the chocolate at precise temperatures so the cocoa butter crystallized into the right form. Dark chocolate, the page said, was worked at thirty-one to thirty-two degrees Celsius. Elizabeth had chosen milk, because the milk rounds were the size of dinner plates and there were more of them, and she was seventeen and did not yet believe that instructions had to match the material.

The kitchen on Saturday mornings was loud with other work. Sage was at the sink decanting soup into quart containers, arguing with Kassidy about whether the school board was a plutocracy because three of its members owned the developments being built where the old stadium stood. Sage said yes, obviously; Kassidy said the word lost its meaning if you used it that way. Elizabeth found she cared about the argument and could not follow it, because her thermometer was reading thirty-one and a half and she was stirring in careful figure eights, waiting for the shine.

She dipped a spoon and laid it on the counter beside the window, where it was coolest. They waited. The chocolate stayed dull and wet, refusing to tack up, and when she touched it her fingertip came away smeared. She tried again through the whole morning, holding the bowl at thirty-one, then thirty-two, watching the thermometer the way Sage's mother watched lottery numbers. Nothing set. The second batch bloomed with pale streaks that looked like frost, though it had never been near a freezer.

"You're staring at it like it owes you money," Kassidy said, leaning over her shoulder.

"It worked for Ms. Robinson last week. The dark stuff. It snapped, it was perfect." Elizabeth turned the printed page over, then the page under it, from a different site, and there it was in a paragraph she had skipped: milk chocolate is tempered to a lower working temperature than dark, around twenty-nine to thirty degrees Celsius, because the milk fat softens the cocoa butter. She read it twice. "I've been running it four degrees too hot the entire time. The whole morning."

Sage abandoned the soup containers and came to look, drying her hands on her jeans. "So it's not that you're bad at it. It's that the recipe was for the wrong material."

"The recipe was for dark. I never even thought about it." Elizabeth felt something atavistic in her relief, the old animal gratitude of finding out that the fault was in the world and not in yourself. She set a new pot of water to simmer, chopped a fresh round of milk chocolate, and began again, keeping her voice flat as she narrated the numbers so she would not jinx them. Twenty-nine and a half. She held it there, stirring, until her wrist ached.

The spoon test transfixed all three of them. Within a minute the coating lost its wet look and turned satin, then glassy, and when Elizabeth flexed the spoon the chocolate broke with a clean, dry sound, like a small bone of light. Sage made her do it again just to hear it. Kassidy took a photograph of the shard on the windowsill, and Ms. Robinson, passing with a tray of empty jars, stopped and looked and asked how she had gotten it right after the morning's failures.

Elizabeth opened her mouth to explain and found she had to be careful, because part of what she wanted to say was that she had trusted a set of instructions more than she had trusted the evidence in front of her, and that this seemed like something larger than chocolate, and she was not sure yet whether it was. Instead she said, "Milk runs cooler than dark. Twenty-nine to thirty. I had it too hot." She dipped the next spoon and laid it on the sill, and the three of them leaned in to watch it set.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The truck's passenger seat had a crack running down the middle of it, and Maelie kept her knees pulled up so her sneakers wouldn't get caught in it. Her father drove. Behind them, in the trailer hitched to the truck, most of her life was boxed and labeled in her mother's handwriting, which was neater than anyone's in the family and therefore had been assigned to all the labels. Nine hours to Corringham. She had counted the boxes once, in the driveway, and then stopped, because counting them felt like rumination and she had promised herself she would not do that today.

Kiefer had ridden with them for the first two hours, as far as the toll plaza outside Dunmore, where his older brother was waiting to drive him back for his shift at the garden center. He had spent the whole ride arguing with her about whether she was allowed to be sad. "You're going to a whole new city," he kept saying. "There are people there. Statistically there have to be people you'd like." And Maelie kept saying, "That's not the same as Nika," and Kiefer kept saying, "Obviously," in the tone of someone who thought he had won the argument and hadn't.

At the toll plaza they'd had a real goodbye, the awkward kind where you both reach out and then change your mind about hugging and end up shaking hands like business partners. Kiefer had pressed something into her palm during the handshake: a folded page torn from a notebook. She'd waited until the truck was back on the highway to open it.

The note was in Kiefer's terrible handwriting, which slanted downhill as though written on a ship. It said: "In psych last spring Ms. Tan made us read about this researcher, Jeffrey Hall. He did a study in 2018 where he figured out how much time it actually takes to make a friend. His estimate was more than 200 hours spent together before people became close friends. I looked at that number and thought of you and Nika and how you basically lived at each other's houses for four years. You already put in the hours once, so you can probably do it again. But also don't do it again too well or I'll be jealous. Text me from the toll road. K."

She read it three times. She did the math against her fingers, quietly, so her father wouldn't ask. Four years of shared lunches, of Saturday afternoons, of Nika's basement and its broken piano, of the summer they'd repainted the shed and gotten blue paint in each other's hair. Thousands of hours, easily. It was almost insulting, how large the number was, and also, in a strange way, the first kind thing anyone had said to her all week. It meant the weight of what she was leaving had a measurement. It also meant that in Corringham she was starting from zero, and that the girl who would sit next to her in some classroom in September had no idea she was holding a debt of two hundred unpaid hours.

She texted Nika instead of Kiefer. "Did Ms. Tan assign you the Hall thing too?" The reply came before the next exit: a photo of the same study, dog-eared, with a sticky note in Nika's writing that said DEPRESSING, and beneath it, in smaller letters, except for us probably. Maelie laughed out loud, a short bark of a laugh that made her father glance over.

"What's funny?"

"Nika thinks a friendship study is depressing."

"Is that the class where they teach you about mutualism?" her father asked. He was trying, in his saturnine, half-frowning way, to be cheerful, and she let him have it. "Where two things help each other out so both survive?"

"That's biology, Dad. But close enough."

They stopped at a rest area with a vending machine that ate her dollar, and she had to stand there negotiating with it while a line formed behind her, and a toddler in the line announced to everyone, with great authority, "It's broken," which somehow made the whole line laugh and made her feel, briefly and illogically, like she was already among her people. She got the chips on the second try. The toddler looked vindicated.

Back in the truck, with Corringham two hours away, she wrote out two messages and deleted both. To Kiefer: something about the hours, something grateful, but every version sounded like a graduation speech. To Nika: something about starting over, but every version sounded like a goodbye, and she didn't want a goodbye, she wanted a see you at Thanksgiving, which Nika had already texted twice without her asking. She put the phone face down on her knees and watched the guardrail run past, counting the posts the way she'd counted the boxes, and this time she let herself.

The houses began to thicken along the road, then the streets, then a water tower with CORRINGHAM in fading letters. Her father turned into the new driveway, gravel popping under the tires, and sat for a moment with his hands still on the wheel. "Ready?" he asked. Maelie looked at the front door, at the blank windows, at a kid down the street already watching them from a porch with the unconcealed curiosity of someone her own age.

"One second," she said, and picked up the phone again. To Nika, she typed: "First person I meet here, I'm starting a timer. Two hundred hours. You're on the clock too." Then she opened her door and stepped down into the gravel.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
Mr. Addo set the assignment on Tuesday like a man laying down a card he knew would lose him the hand: two scholarly articles on the same question, compared, weighed, judged. "A critical review," he said, tapping the rubric, "not a book report with two books. You have to decide which one you believe, and tell me why." Daniel copied the deadline into his planner in his smallest handwriting, the handwriting reserved for things he intended to survive.

The question he chose was whether later school start times actually improved adolescent sleep, which felt fitting, since he was writing it at eleven at night. The database gave him two articles in twenty minutes, and he felt the particular insouciance of a student whose work is essentially finished. One was from a pediatrics journal, dense with tables. The other was shorter, livelier, posted on something called a repository, with a banner across the top he did not read closely. He read both, took notes in two colors, and arrived at Kyle's locker on Thursday prepared to say the assignment was easy.

"It's not easy," said Ophelia, who was crouched at the neighboring locker retrieving a fallen pen. "Mine were about the same thing, screen time, and one of them said the opposite of the other. Also, one of them was a preprint."

"A what?"

"A preprint. It's a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings haven't been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal." She said it the way people recite things they looked up at one in the morning, flat and slightly triumphant.

Daniel went home and found the banner he had not read. On it, in gray type, was the word Ophelia had used. His livelier article, the one with the better sentences and the more satisfying conclusion, had never appeared in a journal at all.

He sat with that for a while. The window of his room gave onto the neighbor's yard, where a sprinkler ticked through its arc with mechanical patience. He opened the preprint again and read the methods section, then the journal article's methods section, then both again, side by side, the way Mr. Addo had gesticulated at the board, one hand for each source, as though weighing fruit. The preprint studied four hundred students over one term. The journal article studied four thousand over three years. The preprint's findings were bolder. He began to see why unchecked findings might be bolder, and then stopped himself, because that was not a reason to disbelieve them either. Boldness was not the same as mendacity, and neither was the same as truth.

In class on Monday, Mr. Addo moved among the desks asking a single question of each student: which article did you trust? When he reached Ophelia, she said, "The journal one, obviously," and Mr. Addo wrote something on his clipboard and said nothing, which was somehow worse than an argument.

When he reached Daniel, Daniel heard himself say, "The journal one has better evidence, but the preprint is asking a question the journal one doesn't." His own voice sounded uncertain to him and he let it. "The review I can't write is the one where I pretend one of them is worthless." Mr. Addo looked at him for a moment longer than was comfortable, then moved on to Kyle, who had printed his articles in a font so large they resembled picture books.

Daniel revised at the library during lunch, the table under his elbows smelling faintly of someone else's hand sanitizer. He wrote a paragraph about the preprint's limits, then a paragraph about what it did that the journal article wouldn't, then a sentence he liked and immediately distrusted, about how the absence of checking was not the presence of error. He crossed out the sentence. He wrote it again with one word changed. Outside, a groundskeeper was dragging a hose across the quad, and the sprinkler of Tuesday's night had become this new small theater of water and labor, and Daniel, watching it without knowing he watched it, underlined the changed sentence.

Ophelia dropped into the chair across from him with her sandwich half unwrapped. "So which one do you believe?" she asked.

"I'll tell you when I'm done being wrong about it," Daniel said, and turned back to the page, pen hovering above the last empty line.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981.
story:
Megan arrived at the community garden at eight forty, ten minutes early, which she regretted immediately because early meant standing alone by the gate with nothing to do but read the laminated sign about composting. The garden occupied a corner lot behind the old legion hall, three dozen raised beds framed in untreated spruce, and at the far end, under a canopy of white poly, volunteers were setting up folding tables for the food bank's Saturday distribution. She had signed up because her mother had said it would look good on applications, and because she had wanted, obscurely, to feel like a person who did this kind of thing, a person whose goodness was not merely theoretical.

Mr. Adeyemi, who ran the garden and the food bank out of the same trailer, handed her a clipboard and a pair of gloves with holes at two fingertips. "You'll weigh the produce," he said. "Greens from the beds, whatever the donation boxes bring. Write the number, don't round it." He said it without ceremony, the way you'd tell someone how to work a hose, and Megan understood that she had expected some kind of ceremony, some acknowledgment of her rectitude, and had been gently refused it.

Malakai from her economics class was already at the weighing table, sorting bruised tomatoes into one crate and passable ones into another. "I didn't know you did this," he said, not unpleasantly. She said she was new, and he nodded toward a bin of yellowing chard. "That's gone. Smell it." She leaned in and caught something faintly noxious, a swampy sweetness, and pushed the bin off the scale into the compost row. "You get good at telling," Malakai said. "Sad lettuce from sleeping lettuce. Sleeping lettuce is fine."

Between customers, an older woman with a wheeled cart asked how long the food bank had been operating, and Malakai said the garden one was only five years old, but the organization went way back. "Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981," he said, pulling a crate of carrots toward him. "Which is nothing. That's like, my parents' lifetime." Megan repeated the date to see if it would change shape in her mouth. Nineteen eighty-one. She had assumed food banks were as old as libraries, something a country simply had. That they were newer than VCRs rearranged something in her thinking, though she could not yet say what.

At eleven a pickup truck delivered boxes from the grocery store, and among the bread and dented cans was a letter, sealed and addressed to "The Volunteers," which the driver said had been taped to the donation bin. Megan opened it with the tip of a pen. The handwriting was small and forward-leaning. I am writing to apologize for the state of the zucchini I left last week. I knew they were soft when I put them in. It was wrong of me to treat your table as a place to hide what I did not want. I have enclosed ten dollars for the compost. Please do not try to find me. I am seventy-four and it was ten zucchini. Megan read it twice, then handed it to Malakai, who laughed, then stopped laughing and read it again. "She paid for the compost," he said. "She wanted to be exculpated." Megan said she thought the woman mostly wanted to be honest, and they stood there disagreeing mildly, without heat, the way they disagreed in class.

A boy of maybe nine came through the line with his grandmother and, while she chose potatoes, stood at Megan's scale and asked what the numbers were for. She showed him how the display flickered and settled, and let him weigh a beet in each hand, one in each of his palms, guessing first. He guessed four hundred grams for the left one and it came out at three ninety-two, and he looked up at her with such pure astonishment at his own accuracy that she felt something loosen in her chest. She had spent the morning half-asking whether charity was a system for feeding people or a system for letting other people feel clean, and the boy with the beet did not answer the question, but he made both versions of the morning true at once.

At noon Mr. Adeyemi made tea in the trailer and they drank it standing in the doorway, looking at the beds. "You'll come back?" he asked, and Megan said yes before she had fully decided, and then realized that saying it had decided her. She still didn't know whether the garden fed hunger or only softened it, whether a country that invented food banks in 1981 had solved a problem or given it a permanent address. Malakai wiped the scale with a rag and said the next Saturday he'd teach her the onion rule, which he refused to explain in advance.

The last customers were leaving when Megan noticed the woman with the wheeled cart still by the gate, reading the composting sign. Megan walked over and asked if she'd found what she needed. The woman said she was taking notes, that her building had a courtyard going to waste. "Sunflowers," she said, tapping the sign. "They say sunflowers pull the bad stuff out of the ground." She clicked her pen, wrote one more word, and rolled the cart toward the bus stop.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
Henry arrived at the rink early enough to hear the Zamboni, and he stood at the glass while it laid down its long wet ribbon, because after tonight he wasn't sure when he would stand there again. His father found him by the boards and put a hand on his shoulder without saying anything, which was its own kind of sentence. Above the far bleachers hung the league banner, five interlocked rings copied in faded paint, blue and yellow and black and green and red on white, and Henry looked at it longer than he meant to.

Faye and Miah came in together, scarves up to their chins, and found him in the third row. His cousin was already there with two of his friends, and the whole bench of them settled in as the teams came out for warmups. Henry's old team. He had been their goalie until two weeks ago, until the semifinal, until the puck came off a skate in the last minute and he was moving the wrong way and it went in under his glove. He had not been cut. He had simply stopped coming, and the coach had not called, and the silence had arranged itself around him like a verdict.

"It's weird without you down there," Faye said, unwrapping a chocolate bar and breaking off half for him.

"It's not weird," Miah said. "It's exactly the same, just in a different net."

That was Miah's way, trenchant and quick, and Henry half admired it and half flinched, because the truth delivered that cleanly left no room to argue with it. He took the chocolate anyway. Below them the goalie in his old crease made the first save of warmups, a routine catch, glove up and settled, and a small warm patch of pride surprised him by arriving before the bitterness did.

While the anthems played, Faye leaned over. "Do you know why the rings are those colors?" she asked. "I have a bet with Miah. I say it's random."

"It's not random," Henry said, and then found he didn't know what it actually was. He pulled out his phone, shielding it against the cold light, and searched with his thumb. There it was. A French baron, Pierre de Coubertin, had designed the five rings in 1913, and he had chosen the colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background. He read it twice.

"Every flag back then had at least one of those colors in it somewhere," he told Faye. "Even the white. He picked them so nobody would be left out."

"See," Faye said to Miah, and held out her palm, and Miah slapped a toonie into it, muttering that Henry had clearly looked it up and the bet was corrupted. Henry smiled and looked back at the banner. Nobody left out. It was a nice idea, five circles wide. He thought about his own name, which had stopped appearing in the group chat, and about how a design could promise inclusion and still not manage it, and how maybe the promise and the failure weren't even the same argument.

Between periods, with the score 1-1, he went out to the lobby where the cold was less sharp and read the message that had come an hour ago, before he'd decided to come at all. It was from Miah, sent at 5:41. "Nobody thinks what you're doing is an indictment of you or them. You don't need the team to lose to exculpate you and you don't need them to win to feel worse. Come watch the game with us. That's the whole ask." He stood with the phone in both hands, breath fogging the screen, and understood that Miah had seen through him days ago, and had waited anyway, and had not said a word at the rink because Miah understood that some things a person has to walk toward on his own.

Inside, the third period had started without him. He climbed back to his seat between Faye and his father. The pace had gone desperate, bodies along the boards, the new goalie holding the crease the way Henry used to, and Henry caught himself tracking the rebounds out loud, quietly, the way you root for a person you have decided to forgive. With four minutes left his old team drew a penalty, and during the whistle his father leaned over and said, close to his ear, "You could come to practice Tuesday. Just once. Nobody's asking for more than that."

Henry watched the faceoff circle empty, the wingers crouching in, the puck dropped and instantly swallowed in a tangle of sticks.

"Maybe Tuesday," he said, and then the puck squirted loose to the point, and everyone in the third row stood up screaming.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
Katherine spread the county maps across the library table and weighted the corners with Nicholas's pencil case. The assignment from Ms. Chanthavong was due Friday: model how their town's growth over thirty years would affect its water supply. Nicholas had already claimed the graphics. Angelo, who actually lived next to the reservoir, had the field data. That left Katherine with the hard part, the part nobody wanted, which was figuring out how anything connected to anything else.

"I can draw the town at three different sizes," Nicholas said, tapping the map. "Now, twice this, triple this."

"That's not a model, that's a coloring exercise." She pulled her laptop toward her. "If the town doubles, the water use doubles. But so does the runoff pollution, and so does the tax base, and the tax base pays for the treatment plant that fixes the pollution. It all feeds back on itself."

Angelo leaned over from the next seat. "So build it in the spreadsheet. Population times gallons per person."

"That's one line. I need the whole web." She was already searching: town growth model, feedback, water. Most of what came back was real estate listings. She tried systems, resources, and on the second page found a scan of an old report with a plain gray cover.

She read the first pages twice. The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team. They had wanted to know whether growth could continue forever, and instead of guessing, they had built a computer model. The model was called World3, and it linked five things: population, food, industry, pollution, resources. Not one at a time. All five, pushing and pulling each other. She sat back. Somebody in 1972 had already done, on mainframes the size of rooms, exactly the assignment Ms. Chanthavong had handed a sixteen-year-old with a school Chromebook.

"Found something?" Nicholas asked.

"It's called World3," she said. "It linked population, food, industry, pollution and resources. One system. That's what we're missing."

"So copy it."

"I can't. It was the whole world." She turned the laptop so he could see the diagram, arrows looping everywhere. "But the shape of it works. Population, industry, pollution, resources, and instead of food, water. Our town in miniature."

Angelo came around the table and studied the loops. "Where's the reservoir in all that?"

"Resources. And pollution loops back into it, because the runoff from all the new roads goes somewhere." She started sketching boxes on the back of Nicholas's map, arrows curving between them, water feeding population, population feeding industry, industry feeding pollution, pollution choking the water. Her hand slowed on the last arrow. "This is where it gets ugly. Every loop I draw makes the next one worse."

Ms. Chanthavong circulated through the library, stopped at their table, and rested a finger on the photocopy of the gray cover. "You found that in the school's basement collection, I take it. Half our library is legacy material nobody checks out." She moved on before Katherine could ask whether legacy meant forgotten or discredited.

By Thursday night the three of them were in Katherine's kitchen, the spreadsheet glowing on the counter, her father periodically expostulating from the doorway that a school project did not require the oven timer, the calculator app, and every pot lid in the house arranged as props. Nicholas was defending his graphs. "People will look at this and only see the doomsday part. We should cut the pollution loop."

"You can't cut a loop because it's inconvenient," Katherine said. "That's the whole point of the model. You leave one arrow out and you're lying."

"It's extrinsic, though," Nicholas argued. "The runoff isn't our project. Ms. Chanthavong said water supply."

"It becomes water supply the second it's in the reservoir." Angelo slid his field notes across the counter. "I took samples after the last storm. turbidity's up. That's your link, not hypothetical."

They ran it three ways before midnight. Steady growth and the reservoir failed in year nineteen of the model. Slow growth and it held, barely, with rationing in dry years. Aggressive industry, the version the town council had actually proposed, and the crash came in eleven. Katherine stared at that last number while Nicholas packed up and Angelo texted his mother for a ride. In World3 the MIT team had faced the same wall, she was fairly sure, though the scan hadn't shown her every run. What she couldn't determine, sitting on the kitchen floor at one in the morning with her chin on the counter, was which of her arrows the real town would obey. Her model said growth had a price. The town's whole lineage, the founders' names on the mill plaque, the assumption that her own street had once been a field and would always keep sprouting new streets behind it, said the opposite. Both could not be true forever. Neither she nor the model could say when forever ended.

On Friday she stood at the front with the pot lids stacked behind her like a shrine. "In 1972, an MIT team published The Limits to Growth for the Club of Rome," she began, and clicked to the diagram, five boxes and a web of arrows, and then to her own version, redrawn overnight, one box relabeled in her handwriting. "This is us," she said, and tapped the screen.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Automation bias is the tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems and to ignore contradicting information, even when that information is correct.
story:
The app had flagged Mia on Tuesday, and by Wednesday the schedule had already desiccated into a single name where hers used to be. Isla saw it when she clocked in: the shifts all reassigned, Mia's column blank, and at the bottom of the manager's screen a red banner reading CONFIDENCE: 94 percent. The system watched the register through a camera above the pastry case, and it had decided that Mia's mannerism of tucking her receipt pad under her arm was, in fact, her concealing one.

"He won't even look at the till report," Mia said from the corner table, where she sat with a coffee she hadn't paid for because nobody would let her pay for anything anymore. "I told him to count the drawer. He said the drawer doesn't matter."

Isla had counted the drawer herself, after close, kneeling behind the counter with the door chained. It balanced to the cent, both nights the app had flagged. She had the printout folded in her apron pocket, warm as contraband.

The manager arrived at four with a flat white and his phone mounted on the dashboard of his attention. He was not a cruel man; he was, in Isla's private taxonomy, a man who had outsourced his judgment the way other people outsource their laundry. "The model looks at hundreds of videos," he said, when she set the printout beside his cup. "It sees things we can't."

"It sees things that aren't there," Isla said. "The drawer balances. I counted it twice."

"The drawer is one data point." He tapped the phone. In its window, a small blue arrow moved along a street.

That was when Ms. Bondarenko came in for her small black, which she drank at the window with a paperback she never finished. She had heard enough, apparently, because she set the book down and said, "My sister did that last month. Drove her niece to a swim meet." The GPS had routed her down Halton Road, which the city had closed for repaving. "Signs all along it, orange signs, and cones, and a man in a vest waving his arms." Her sister had followed the voice anyway, right up to the barrier, and then sat there asking the phone to recalculate. "A machine said turn left, so she turned left. It didn't matter what her own eyes were telling her."

Isla turned that over while she steamed milk. A woman in a car, ignoring information that was correct and right in front of her, because a screen had suggested otherwise. It wasn't stupidity; the sister taught piano and did her own taxes. It was something about where the authority had gone, some quiet seismic shift in who got believed. She pulled the printout from her apron and smoothed it on the counter in front of the manager.

"The till report is the road sign," she said. "The app is the GPS. You're driving at the cones."

"The comparison is flattering," the manager said, but he looked at the paper longer this time, long enough that his thumb stopped moving on the phone.

"It's called automation bias," Isla said. "Favoring what the automated system says over information that contradicts it, even when the contradicting information is right."

"Where'd you read that?"

"Your banner says ninety-four percent confidence. It doesn't say ninety-four percent accuracy." She had looked it up at one in the morning, phone propped against a mug of chamomile, after Mia had texted a row of ellipses and then nothing. The distinction had seemed, at one in the morning, almost unbearably important, and it still did.

Mia came over from the corner with her cup, which was now empty, which Isla noticed the way one notices a small promise. "So what happens now?" Mia asked, and it was a fair question, because Isla didn't entirely know. The drawer balanced, and the sister's car had stopped at the barrier, but barriers got moved and tills got recounted, and somewhere in a data center the model was still watching the pastry case, still learning from videos that now included Mia standing at the counter demanding her job. Isla believed the printout. She also believed the next version of the app would have a newer banner.

The manager folded the paper in half, then in quarters, and put it in his shirt pocket instead of the bin, which was not justice but was, for a Tuesday in a coffee shop, movement. "I'll rerun the audit," he said.

"Count the drawer yourself," Isla said. "With your hands."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
story:
Tyson had blocked the whole one-act on graph paper before he ever stepped into the theatre, each X and O marching across the grid like troops with a plan. Ms. Rodríguez had handed him the script in September and said the words he kept returning to: "Directing is mostly deciding where people stand." That had seemed simple then. Now the actors were late, the rehearsal slot had shrunk to ninety minutes, and the room was not the room he had planned for.

The community theatre's main stage was being refinished, so Ms. Rodríguez had moved them into the black box down the hall, and in the black box the chairs didn't face one way. They ringed the playing space on all four sides. Tyson stood in the centre of the empty square with his graph paper and felt the paper go useless in his hands. Every entrance he had drawn came from "stage left," which meant nothing here, or meant four different things depending on where you sat.

"You're staring at that paper like it insulted you," Victor said, dropping his bag by the door. Victor played the brother, the larger role, and he had opinions about everything, most of them loud.

"Blocking's wrong," Tyson said. "All of it."

"So fix it. We have until seven."

Derrick arrived second, apologizing for the bus, and the girl who played the mother came in a few minutes after, still in her work apron. Tyson looked at the four of them standing in a loose clump and then at the chairs. He made them sit down, all four sides, one row each, so the seats would have faces in them. "You're the audience," he said. "Tell me when you're looking at someone's back."

They ran the opening scene as written on his paper, and it failed almost immediately. Victor delivered his longest speech facing the north chairs, which meant the south, east and west sections watched his shoulder blades shift. Derrick raised a hand from the south row. "I haven't seen his face in like a minute." A girl in the east row didn't even raise a hand; she just said, "Nothing's happening over here."

So that was the problem stated plainly. On a stage like this the audience sat on all sides, and Tyson had to keep the actors moving so no section spent the whole play looking at backs. It wasn't a flaw in his drawings so much as a different physics. He wondered, walking the perimeter, whether the old directors had felt this the first time, the strange realization that there was no front, that the room had no single way to be looked at.

He stopped trying to preserve his graph paper. Instead he gave Victor a rule: never plant your feet for more than a line and a half, and when you turn, turn. The long monologue became a slow circle, so that each side of chairs got the face for part of it. When two actors had to talk to each other, he pulled them apart on a diagonal, faces angled outward like the corners of a square, so the conversation reached everyone as profile. Some of it felt awkward and some of it, when it clicked, looked better than anything on his original plan. The scene where the mother leaves, which he had staged as a flat walk upstage, became a crossing through the centre, and the west chairs, who would have watched her hair the whole way, got her face as she went.

The set pieces were a separate disaster. The painted backdrop, a wide horizon of yellowed grass meant to suggest a steppe under a wide sky, was built to hang behind a stage that had a behind. Here it would hide half the actors from two whole sections. Tyson turned it flat to the floor, laid down as cracked ground, which looked like nothing until Derrick knelt on it and a flake of paint came away on his knee, the old surface gone friable from years in the storage loft. They would have to lay down tarps or repaint, and there was no money for paint.

"Can we just beguile them with the acting and skip the scenery?" Victor asked, and Tyson said maybe, and Ms. Rodríguez, passing through on her way to the office, paused at the door and watched the diagonal scene without comment, then kept walking, which Tyson chose to take as approval. He still didn't know if the circle monologue would hold up with a real audience, or whether ninety minutes a night was enough to relearn a play they had all thought they knew. He taped a fresh square of paper to the wall, drew a box with arrows, and wrote at the top: ROUND. Then he called them back to places.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.
story:
The posterboard had cost nine dollars, which Amy intended to amortize across at least four future science fairs, and she was drawing the ribosome as a smiling hamburger bun when Adelyn arrived with a shoebox of paper codons and her whole face set to panic.

"We have a problem," Adelyn said, dumping the codons on the kitchen table. "Steven tested our game. He got garbage."

The game was Amy's little brother's fault, technically. He had watched her muttering about central dogma for two weeks and asked whether DNA was like a recipe, and she had said more like a library where you photocopy one page and take the copy to a kitchen, and he had said that sounded boring, and she had said fine, we'll make it a game, and somehow that had become a shoebox, eighty-one paper slips, a plastic tub labeled RIBOSOME, and a science fair deadline on Thursday.

Steven came over after dinner with his test results, which was a sheet of paper with amino acid letters that spelled, when he'd matched everything up, absolutely nothing. "It's gibberish," he said. "Your game is broken. Or biology is broken."

"Both are possible," Amy said, and took the sheet.

The rules were simple, or they should have been. The DNA strand unzips; transcription makes an mRNA copy with U instead of T; then the mRNA slides through the ribosome three letters at a time, and every three-letter codon matches one amino acid, which was the whole point, the whole miracle, a cipher that every living thing on earth had agreed to use since before there were trees. Mr. Çelik had shown them the codon chart on Monday, tacked it to the board, and said only, "The chart does not lie. If your answer is nonsense, the problem is upstream of the chart," which Amy had found unbearably smug at the time and now found possibly prophetic.

She spread the mRNA out on the table. AUGGCCAAUGCC. Steven had started at the first letter and read AUG, GCC, AAU, GCC, which gave methionine, alanine, asparagine, alanine, which was not gibberish, actually, which was annoying, because his second attempt had started one letter later and produced UGC, CAA, UGC, C, a trailing orphan letter and a nonsense word that had made him throw the pen.

"Wait," Amy said. "Which one did you submit?"

"The second one. The first one felt too easy. I thought the AUG was, like, decoration."

Last summer flashed back to her, unbidden: her uncle teaching her to drive stick in the church parking lot, telling her that first gear wasn't optional, that you couldn't just start in third and hope. She had argued with him for twenty minutes, an intransigent seventeen-year-old certain that gears were a suggestion, until the car stalled twice and he laughed so hard he had to hold the door. She had changed her mind about gears, slowly, in the way you change your mind about things you lose arguments about.

Amy turned the paper over and wrote the fact as it had surfaced somewhere in Tuesday's homework: "Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine." She held it up. "It's not decoration. It's first gear."

"Where does it say that?" Steven demanded.

"The chart. Monday. Mr. Çelik circled it and everything." She hadn't written it down at the time because she'd been drawing a duck in her margin, a fact she chose not to volunteer.

Adelyn was already re-sorting the paper slips, sliding the mRNA through the plastic tub. "So the message doesn't start wherever you feel like it. It starts at AUG. Met, alanine, asparagine, alanine." She looked up. "That's the answer. Steven's first try was right and he threw away the pen."

"I did throw away the pen," Steven admitted. "That was dramatic of me."

Amy's little brother wandered in, drawn by the possibility of snacks, found the kitchen's hedonism limited to saltines, and stayed anyway to watch them rebuild the game with a green slip marked START pinned to the AUG codon. He demanded to test it. He read down the strip, hit the green slip, said "start," and decoded four amino acids without a single nonsense word, then looked up with the expression of a boy who suspected he had been given an educational experience disguised as a game and was deciding whether to complain.

"So every protein starts with methionine," Adelyn said, sorting slips back into the box. "Every single one?"

"Usually," Amy said. She liked the word usually. It was honest in a way her uncle's gears hadn't been, an admission that the system had exceptions she didn't yet understand, that the whole beautiful cipher had asterisks. She was going to put that on the poster, the caveat, the small print of life, and Mr. Çelik would probably nod at it in his smug way and she would probably let him.

"Thursday," Steven said, stacking the shoebox. "Green slip, AUG, methionine, first gear. I can memorize four things."

"Three things," said her brother, taking a saltine. "The fourth thing is a car."

Amy pinned the START slip to the posterboard, stepped back, and tilted her head at the smiling hamburger bun. "Okay," she said, "but hear me out. What if the ribosome has a hat."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.
story:
Mr. Das did not start the car. He sat with his hands folded on his knees, in the passenger seat of the little driving school hatchback, and watched Alexia adjust the mirror for the second time.

"Buckle up," he said.

She had her hand on the ignition, and it stayed there. Outside, the long gravel driveway ran down to the country road, where a tractor moved so slowly it might have been parked. She reached for the belt, then stopped, because a point was forming and she wanted to make it first. "We're still in the driveway," she said. "We haven't even turned onto the road."

"And we won't," said Mr. Das, "until you're belted."

The previous September, her mother had sat on the porch steps with a letter from the insurance company and read it aloud in a voice she saved for bank correspondence. The letter said that if Alexia took driver's training through a certified school, the company would indemnify them against certain damages, and her mother had found the phrase so beautiful she'd said it twice, as if it were a line of poetry instead of fine print. Her father was on sabbatical that year, which everyone explained as a rest from teaching and which Alexia had privately come to understand as a rest from her mother reading letters aloud. It was a household of careful people. Careful people, she had noticed, were very relaxed about the things they did out of habit, and extremely tense about the things they had to decide on purpose.

"I know it's the rule," she said now. "I just think rules should have reasons attached."

"Good," said Mr. Das. "Then you'll like this one." He didn't say anything else. The tractor on the road had actually progressed, she could see, by about the length of a car. A crow landed on the mailbox and reconsidered.

She pulled the belt across anyway, because she wanted to drive more than she wanted to win, and clicked it home. "There."

"There," he agreed. He set the key in the ignition himself and turned it, and the engine made its small dutiful sound. "Now, before you put it in gear, tell me what you know about seat belts. Not the rule. The reason."

She looked down the driveway. There was a curve at the bottom where the gravel met the asphalt, and her plan, formed over three nights of studying the manual in bed, was to take it at walking speed. "Something like half," she said slowly. "I read that wearing one cuts serious crash injuries and deaths by about half. It was a CDC statistic. I memorized it for the written test and then I forgot I'd memorized it, which is apparently how my memory works."

"About half," Mr. Das confirmed. "Serious crash-related injuries and deaths, according to the CDC. Reduced by about half." He said it flat, like a man reading a speed limit sign. "So the reason is attached."

She put the car in gear, and it moved, and the gravel crackled under the tires like something being crumpled in another room. Half. She turned this over as the mailbox slid past. Half was a strange number to sit with, because it wasn't a promise. It didn't say you'd be fine. It said that if the worst thing happened, the belt gave you a coin-flip better than the one you'd had without it, and that was all anyone could hand you before you pulled onto a road. Her mother's beautiful letter had been like that too: the company would cover certain damages. Certain. Everyone kept handing her almosts.

At the end of the driveway she stopped, checked both ways, and waited for a truck that was still half a field away, because she was not going to be casual about anything today, possibly ever.

"You can go," said Mr. Das. "The truck is a geological event, not a vehicle."

She pulled out. The road opened ahead, two lanes with a faded yellow line and hedgerows leaning toward each other overhead. The steering wheel did something small and alive under her hands, correcting her without asking, and she corrected back. Twenty miles an hour felt like a held breath.

"I still think it's pernicious," she said, "the way habits make you obey without ever telling you why. The belt thing. I almost argued with you back there and I couldn't have said what the belt actually does. Statistically."

"Most people can't," said Mr. Das. He adjusted his mirror, the way a man does when he's pleased and doesn't want it noticed. "Faster bit, coming up. Ease onto the gas."

She eased. The hedgerows began to move.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs: during the US recession of the early 1980s, unemployment rose above 10 percent.
story:
Sydney had told everyone, twice, that she had the interview under control. She said it again in the food court, wedged between Milla and Siena and three trays of untouched pretzel bites, because saying it out loud made it truer. The internship at the credit union paid actual money and required only one thing of her: a five-minute explanation, to a panel of strangers, of how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had a week. She had, according to her, "basically already learned it," which was a sentence she had been saying since Monday without once opening her laptop.

"You could just explain it to us right now," Siena said, flicking a pretzel bite across the table. "Practice. We're strangers. I'm basically a panel."

"You're a stranger to economics, definitely."

"Rude and true," Siena said, and ate the pretzel bite anyway.

Sydney tried. She got as far as "the central bank raises rates, and then, um, people spend less, because money costs more to borrow," and then Milla's straw made a noise like a dying kazoo and the whole sentence collapsed laughing. Milla apologized without meaning it. Siena suggested, with the gentle malice of a true friend, that Sydney go find Ms. Siddiqui, who managed the bookstore on the upper level and had, according to mall legend, once worked at a bank and read everything.

Sydney found her shelving remaindered thrillers, spine out, in a way that suggested the books had personally offended her. Sydney liked Ms. Siddiqui precisely because she never explained anything twice and mostly never explained it once. When Sydney described the interview task, Ms. Siddiqui did not launch into a lecture. She rang up a customer, returned a phone call about invoices, and then said, "My father praises those rate hikes like they were a moral victory. Beat inflation, he says. He kept his job that year. My uncle didn't." She slid the last thriller onto the shelf. "Recession, early eighties. Unemployment went above ten percent." Then she went back to the invoices, which was her way of saying the conversation was over and Sydney's problem now.

Sydney wandered the upper level with her phone out, and here is where the reader should understand that Sydney's account of the next hour cannot be trusted. She would later say she "researched efficiently," and it was technically research, in the sense that she looked things up between games of a tile-matching app. But somewhere between the vape shop and the escalator, the shape of the thing started to assemble itself. Hiking rates was not a magic spell that made prices behave. It worked the way a brake worked, by slowing everything, and when everything slowed, companies sold less, and when companies sold less, they let people go. Her economics teacher had called the trade-off something clinical and forgettable. Ms. Siddiqui's uncle had lived it, or rather lost it, the job, the year everyone else toasted.

Downstairs, Siena and Milla had migrated to the mattress store, lying on display beds like heiresses, and Sydney lay down between them and stared at the ceiling of a mall she had known her whole life. "So the people who praise the hikes," she said slowly, "are usually the people who kept their jobs. That's not an argument. That's luck with a suit on." Milla, face down, said something muffled that might have been agreement or might have been "this mattress is canny with its pricing," which made no sense, but Milla had been reading reviews aloud for twenty minutes and had strong opinions about which store was a racket.

Sydney tried her explanation again, lying there, talking at the fluorescent lights. Raise rates, borrowing costs more, spending cools, demand cools, price rises slow. And the cost of cooling it lands on whoever gets laid off first, and in the early eighties that was enough people that unemployment went above ten percent, a number she could feel now instead of just recite. Siena made her say it twice more, once doing an impression of a panel member falling asleep, once as a game-show host. The game-show version was honestly the best one. Sydney had been an autodidact all week in the sense that she had autodidact-ed nothing, and now, with the pretzel grease barely dry on her hands, she knew the thing well enough to be careful with it, which felt different from knowing it well enough to pass.

She was not going to stand in front of the panel and vilify central bankers, because that was too easy and also not true; she was not going to praise them either, because that was too easy and definitely not true. What she would say, she thought, was that it works, and that it costs, and that the cost is not spread evenly, and that a person giving a five-minute answer ought to admit where the argument gets shaky, like whether the pain is worth it, which smart people still argued about in rooms much fancier than this mall. Whether the panel wanted honesty or wanted confidence, she would find out, and she was, she told Siena, completely calm about that, gripping the escalator rail with both hands on the way down.

Milla chased her to the exit to return the pen she had stolen from the mattress store "for luck." Siena called after her, "Ten percent, Sydney, don't soften it," and Sydney raised the pen over her head like a torch and pushed through the doors into the parking lot heat.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Ms. Kobayashi had written one sentence on the whiteboard she'd wheeled onto the stage: a ten-minute play, drawn from your own life, staged by Friday. Simon sat in the third row of folding chairs with his notebook open and nothing written in it. Around him, classmates called out fragments, arguments with fathers, a cancelled trip, the day a dog died, and he wrote none of them down because none of them were his. He had a life, he was fairly sure, but it refused to arrange itself into anything with a shape.

Jayden sprawled into the seat beside him and read the whiteboard upside down. "Ten minutes," he said. "That's nothing. Mine's about my uncle at Thanksgiving. He's irascible, so it writes itself. He yells at the turkey, my aunt cries, curtain."

"That's not a play," Simon said. "That's an incident."

"It's my incident." Jayden tapped the notebook. "What've you got?"

Simon turned a page he hadn't written on. "There's this thing from economics. Mr. Ferreira spent two weeks on stagflation and my dad kept saying it didn't apply to us, and then the plant cut his hours anyway. I thought maybe that."

"A play about the economy." Jayden considered it. "Nobody claps for that."

They ran the first drafts on Wednesday, on the bare stage with the work lights on, because Ms. Kobayashi believed in hearing things aloud before deciding anything. Jayden went first. He played both his uncle and his aunt, pitching his voice up for the aunt, and the scene did what he'd promised: the uncle raged, the turkey came out dry, the aunt covered her face. Then Jayden ran out of words and stood there, and finally said, "That's it," and walked offstage.

Kiera, sitting cross-legged on the edge of the stage with a pencil in her hair, clapped twice. "It was funny. But nothing changed. He's mad, then he's still mad. What's different at the end?"

"It's a real Thanksgiving," Jayden said. "That's how it went."

"Real things end," Kiera said. "Even that one."

Simon had his notebook out, and he'd written something down during Jayden's scene, a line he half remembered from somewhere, and he read it aloud before he could decide not to. "In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end."

Kiera pointed the pencil at him. "Who told you that?"

"Nobody. It's in the front of the edition Ms. Kobayashi left on the prop shelf. I was looking for a fake telephone." He held up a paperback so cracked its spine was held with a rubber band. "I read the first page last night because I couldn't sleep."

Jayden took the book, flipped it, gave it back. "So my play's missing a third."

"Or it's missing the middle too," Simon said. "The yelling starts and then the yelling stops. Nothing turns it." He heard himself sounding like a teacher and shut up, but the idea had already seated itself: the scene wasn't a whole. It was a fragment wearing a costume.

His own problem was the opposite. Thursday after school, alone in the auditorium, he tried to stage the stagflation scene and found he had too much. His dad at the kitchen table with the letter about reduced hours, the dad's friend Rey arguing it was temporary, the mother quiet at the sink. It ran nineteen minutes and every minute was true and none of them went anywhere. He cut the friend. He cut the sink. He kept cutting until what remained was his father reading the letter aloud, once, badly, and Simon, at twelve, asking whether they were poor, and his father saying, "We're figuring it out," which was not an answer and was somehow still an ending. He read the new draft and found it was seven minutes. The middle had collapsed into a single question. It held, though. He could feel it holding, the way a bridge holds, invisibly, because of what it leaves out.

He staged it Friday. He played his father and asked Kiera to read his own old lines, standing where the audience would be, and under the work lights the scene ran its seven minutes and stopped where it stopped. Nobody clapped right away. Then Ms. Kobayashi said, "Again," and they ran it a second time, and Simon heard, in the second pass, the place where the middle thinned, where his father's voice went flat because Simon didn't actually know what his father had felt, only what he'd said.
