That part he couldn't fix. The play was true to the words and might be false to the man, and no amount of structure would tell him which.

Afterward, in the emptying rows, Jayden dropped into the seat beside him. "Mine's fixed," he said. "The aunt leaves the table at the end. She didn't, in real life, but she should have, and Kiera says that's allowed."

"Is it?"

"That's what I'm asking you."

Simon looked at the whiteboard, at the sentence still on it, at the dark house beyond the work lights where an audience would sit someday and want what Kiera had wanted, for something to change. "I don't know," he said. "I found out what a whole is. I still don't know how much of it has to be true." He closed the rubber-banded book and set it on the seat between them.

Jayden picked it up and read the first page, mouthing the words.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life.
story:
The community studio smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee, and on the first Tuesday of October Ms. Esposito propped a print of Frida Kahlo's Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace against the drying rack. "Today we stop liking things," she said, tapping the glass. "Today we describe them. Colour, composition, symbolism. If you can't describe it, you don't yet see it."

Megan sat between Melia and Calder at the long paint-stained table. She had signed up for the course because it was cheap, and because the flyer in the library had promised scholarship rates for students from indigent households, a phrase she'd read three times before checking the box. Her mother had said it was honest of the studio to admit who the classes were really for. Megan hadn't decided yet whether she agreed.

Melia went first, leaning close to the print. "The background is green, dense, almost no sky. The leaves are darker than anything on her face. So the face is the brightest plane, and the monkey and the cat bracket her shoulders like brackets in an equation." She sat back, pleased with herself, and Ms. Esposito nodded once. "Good. Keep going."

Calder crossed his arms. "This whole method is reactionary," he said. "You want to drag us back to judging lines and balance like it's 1950, so nobody has to talk about what the painting is actually about. She's painting pain. You can't balance-sheet pain." Ms. Esposito didn't argue. "Then show me where the pain is," she said. "Point." Calder pointed at the thorn necklace digging into her neck, at the single drop of blood. "There. That's symbolism. That's form too."

When it was Megan's turn, she stood and found she didn't want to talk about the thorns. "The hummingbird is black," she said, "and it hangs from the necklace like a pendant, and it's dead, and it's the darkest shape in the whole green world. Everything alive around her is watching. Nothing helps." She heard her own voice go thin on the last word, and Calder, to her surprise, didn't pounce.

That night she couldn't sleep, so she did what she'd promised herself she wouldn't do and looked Kahlo up on her phone in bed, the screen too bright against her pillow. She was hunting for the hummingbird's meaning when the date surfaced instead. On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was eighteen, a streetcar crashed into her bus, and the injuries left her in pain for the rest of her life. Megan read it twice. She was eighteen. She had turned eighteen in March, in the back booth of a diner, with Melia stealing her fries. Kahlo had been exactly where she was, standing on some street corner with her whole body still hers.

The next week she brought it up before she could talk herself out of it. "She was our age," Megan said, when Ms. Esposito asked for revisions of their analyses. "In 1925. A streetcar ran into her bus, and after that everything hurt, forever, and the paintings came after. So when we talk about composition, we're talking about someone arranging a body that wouldn't stop hurting." Calder turned in his chair. "So form isn't neutral," he said slowly, as if she'd handed him something. "The arrangement is the argument." Ms. Esposito raised an eyebrow at Megan. "See? You didn't need me to expatiate on that. You needed the date."

Melia wasn't convinced. She argued, on the walk to the bus stop, that making the biography central was its own kind of cage, that Kahlo had studied the old masters and thought in colour wheels and composition whether or not anyone bled for it. Megan walked with her hands in her pockets, holding both ideas and unable to stack one on the other. "Maybe the thorn necklace is about Christ," she said, "and maybe it's about a bus, and maybe she'd laugh at us for choosing." Melia shrugged. "She'd probably paint us choosing."

Back in the studio the following Tuesday, Megan pulled her written critique from her bag and crossed out her opening sentence, the one that called the portrait brave, and wrote above it in the margin: the hummingbird is black and it is the darkest thing here. Then she took the print down from the drying rack and set it on the table where the morning light fell across the dead bird's wings.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 2011 the OPERA experiment reported neutrinos apparently faster than light; in 2012 the result was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light.
story:
The waiting room had the usual pelagic calm of a fish tank in the corner, blue light wobbling over the carpet, and Lauren watched a clownfish trace the same arc it had traced the last three visits. Her mother had dropped her at the clinic door with the phrase "just routine," which had the same effect on Lauren's stomach as the word "minor" has on the description of surgery. Oceanne sat beside her, skipping class for the privilege, flipping a battered magazine. Then Lauren's phone buzzed. Jean-Felix, in block capitals: NEUTRINOS FASTER THAN LIGHT. EINSTEIN WRONG. He'd appended a link to a headline, an exclamation mark, and the message "we are living in the future."

"Slow down," Oceanne said, reading over her shoulder. "What's a neutrino even?"

"Basically nothing. A particle so small it passes through the whole earth without noticing." Lauren tapped the link. The headline was two years of blog reposts away from whatever had actually happened, and she had learned, the hard way, in a class debate about cell phones and cancer, that a headline could be a fossil of a fossil. She typed "OPERA neutrinos" into the search bar, because Jean-Felix's article mentioned the experiment by name and she wanted the primary thing, the bone before the plaster cast.

The first results were from 2011. An experiment in Italy, OPERA, had reported neutrinos that seemed to arrive faster than light would, which, if true, would have upended a century of physics. Lauren read further. Other groups had gone to check. In 2012 the anomaly was traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measuring the same particles found speeds consistent with light. She read it twice, the way she reread a test question that had looked easy and then hadn't. One cable. A loose cable between a detector and a computer, and a headline still travelling the internet years later at its own impossible speed.

"Lauren Walsh," the nurse called, and Lauren went behind the partition, extended her arm, and answered the routine questions while the tourniquet went tight. The needle found its vein on the second try, an idiosyncrasy of her anatomy the nurse noted aloud in a tone that suggested Lauren should be proud of it. "Hold pressure," the nurse said. "A few minutes, so it coagulates properly, then no heavy lifting with that arm." Lauren held the gauze with her free hand and, with the other, typed her reply to Jean-Felix with her thumb.

Oceanne watched her from the waiting room chairs, watched the particular slowness of the typing, and understood that Lauren was doing the thing Oceanne both admired and mildly resented about her, the refusal to let an exciting fact stay exciting until it had been cross-examined. Oceanne knew how the message would be framed before it arrived, because she'd watched Lauren dismantle a rumour about the chemistry teacher with the same patient, apologetic precision. There was a cost to it. Jean-Felix had stopped sending her things for a month after the chemistry episode, and Oceanne had been the one to hear about it at lunch, the sulky monologue, the accusation that Lauren liked being right more than she liked people.

The message arrived: "I looked it up. The experiment was called OPERA, 2011, they reported neutrinos apparently faster than light. In 2012 it got traced to a loose fibre-optic cable, and other experiments measured speeds consistent with light. So Einstein's fine. Sorry." She almost deleted the sorry, then kept it. The reply came back as a single typing bubble that appeared, vanished, appeared again, and finally produced: "you couldn't have let me have it for one afternoon." Lauren put the phone face-down on her knee. In the tank, the clownfish resumed its arc, indifferent to the whole of physics, faster than nothing.

"Ms. Walsh," the doctor said, sliding the curtain back with a folder in her hand. "Your iron's low, not dangerously, and the fainting was likely that plus August heat. We'll supplement and recheck in three months." It was good news dressed in the mild language of the not-yet-settled, one data point awaiting its confirmation, and Lauren found herself trusting it more for admitting that. She flexed her bandaged arm, texted Jean-Felix a single fish emoji, and followed Oceanne out into the parking lot, where the heat hit like a held breath finally released.

"Smoothie," Oceanne said. "You're paying, since you have iron problems now."

"Low iron. There's a difference."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flow through the Florida Straits in the Gulf Stream, a flow oceanographers call 30 sverdrups.
story:
Hudson spread the printed current map across the kitchen table and weighted its curling corners with his mother's teacup and a jar of pens. The map showed the Atlantic in ribbons of red and blue, arrows thick as highways bending away from Florida toward Iceland and Norway. On Monday he had to stand in front of Ms. Park's class and explain how the Gulf Stream kept northern Europe warmer than latitude alone could justify, and at the moment he could not even tell which way the arrows were pointing.

He called Nada because Nada had already done her presentation on monsoons and had survived it. "What did you do when you didn't understand your topic?" he asked.

"I understood my topic," Nada said. "But the night before, I didn't. I stopped trying to explain everything and explained one true thing well." He could hear her eating something crunchy on the other end. "Find the one thing that makes you say wait, really."

The one thing, it turned out, was hiding in a footnote he'd skimmed twice. About 30 million cubic metres of water per second flowed through the Florida Straits, between Florida and Cuba, where the Gulf Stream narrowed and gathered itself. He sat with the number and tried to make it a size. He thought of the town pool, the reservoir on Mahi's road, the flooded creek after the March storm that had excoriated the riverbank and left fence posts leaning like drunks. None of it worked. Thirty million cubic metres of water per second meant nothing he could hold.

Mahi arrived at four with his sister's old globe under one arm, because he'd decided Hudson needed the whole planet to look at and not a flat lie of a map. "Every flat map is an argument," Mahi said, spinning the globe so that Norway faced them. "Your arrows are intransigent on this paper. On the sphere they have to curve." He was right; when Hudson traced the red ribbon onto the globe, it stopped looking like a road and started looking like a slow turning, water swinging north and east and releasing itself into the North Atlantic.

In the margin of the paper, a single word: sverdrups. Hudson searched it and found a unit named for an oceanographer, a way of counting water by the million cubic metres per second. "So this flow," he said slowly, working it out with a pencil against the teacup, "about 30 million cubic metres per second. That's thirty of his units."

"Thirty sverdrups," Mahi said, reading over his shoulder. Hudson wrote the number down and underlined it, and something in the presentation finally had a spine: a fact large enough to carry the rest.

His mother came home at six with groceries and found the table colonized, the teacup exiled to the counter. She didn't scold him. She put a plate of bread and cheese near his elbow without comment, because she had the discernment to know that a boy two days before a presentation was not available for conversation, only for feeding. Mahi's phone buzzed; his father wanted him home. At the door Mahi turned back. "You still can't say why it warms Europe. Only that it does."

"I know," Hudson said. "That's the part that bothers me."

But lying in bed later, he understood something else, that Ms. Park had not asked them for certainty, only for honesty about what they could see and what they couldn't. He could stand up there and give the number, thirty million cubic metres per second through the Florida Straits, thirty sverdrups, and he could show the red ribbon crossing the map, and he could say plainly where his sight ended. Nada's voice came back to him: one true thing, well. He would give the water its size and let the mystery stay a mystery, and he found, testing the sentences in the dark, that this felt less like failure than like standing at the edge of something with his eyes open.

The next morning he rehearsed once in the kitchen while his mother pretended to read the paper. When he got to the part about the Florida Straits, he lifted the teacup off the counter and tipped an imaginary ocean out of it, slow and enormous, and his mother lowered the paper and watched him do it.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
story:
The kitchen of the Marigold had a smell Madison could not stop noticing, cocoa and hot steel and the green bite of scallions from the prep line, and on her second Saturday Mr. Bui set a bowl of chopped chocolate in front of her and said only, "Watch the shine. You will know." She was eighteen, two months from orientation at a college where she intended to study something practical, and she had taken the weekend job because her mother said idle hands, though what she actually wanted, and could not yet say aloud, was to find out whether cooking was chemistry you could eat.

The first batch failed. She melted the chocolate too hot, poured it onto the marble slab Mr. Bui kept for this, and stirred with the scraper while the brown ribbon began to thicken under her hand. It set dull, streaked grey at the edges, and bent instead of snapping when she pressed it with her thumb. Mr. Bui picked up a piece, bent it, put it down, and went back to the walk-in without a word, which was somehow worse than a lecture.

That night Stacey came over with a plastic bag of leftover store-bought chocolate, half a bar she'd been saving, and a problem. "I don't have a marble slab," she said. "Alice keeps saying it's, like, a plutocracy of kitchens, only people with countertops get to temper. I melted mine in the microwave and it just sits there, tacky, like it's sulking." Stacey wanted to dip strawberries for her mother's birthday, and she wanted them to look like the ones in the bakery window, the ones with the hard glassy shell that cracks when you bite it.

Madison had been thinking about something Mr. Bui said in passing, half in Vietnamese to himself, half to her: seeding, he called it, and she'd written the word on the back of her hand in pen. In the flashback that kept returning to her while Stacey talked, Madison was eleven, at her grandmother's sink, watching rock candy grow on a string, and her grandmother said the first crystal teaches the sugar what to be. Madison hadn't understood then. She understood a little more now, though she couldn't have defended the understanding in an argument, and that gap between knowing and being able to say was exactly the thing she kept circling.

"So here," she said, taking Stacey's bag. She chopped the store-bought bar on a cutting board, small and even, the way Mr. Bui had taught her, and stirred the pieces into the bowl of melted chocolate Stacey had brought in a saucepan, still warm. "In the seeding method, the chopped chocolate is already tempered, so it supplies form V crystals for the rest to copy," she said, and heard herself say it and wondered whether she actually knew it or was only repeating it, the way she'd repeated formulas all through calculus without once feeling them. Stacey looked at her. "V like the roman numeral?" "Like the crystal shape, I think. Don't ask me past that."

They stirred. Madison watched the surface, which had begun to undulate strangely, thickening in slow folds as the seed pieces melted away into the mass, and she kept her hand moving because stopping, she had learned the hard way, let the bowl seize. She touched a smear of it to her lower lip, the old test, cooler than skin but not cold. Stacey's phone alarm went off for no reason. Neither of them laughed, and then both of them did.

The strawberries, dipped on newspaper on Stacey's counter, set in twenty minutes with a shine like wet river stone. Stacey snapped a leftover drizzle in half and the sound was clean, a click rather than a bend, and she held the two pieces up like evidence. "Okay," she said. "It worked without the slab. So Alice is wrong, it's not about equipment." "Or it's about having the right kind of leftover," Madison said, and found she meant the question sincerely: how much of any skill was tools, how much was knowledge, how much was the dumb luck of someone having handed you a bar of the right chocolate at the right time. She had changed her mind about something during the stirring, though it was still soft in her, unproven: she had walked into the Marigold believing cooking was following instructions, and now she suspected it was closer to persuasion, coaxing a material toward a shape it was already capable of.

The next Saturday she told Mr. Bui about it, the failed slab batch and the seeded bowl and Stacey's strawberries, and he listened while portioning dough with a bench scraper, his hands moving in their own steady rhythm. He asked her one question, whether the surface had folded when she stirred it, and when she said yes, describing the slow undulating thickening, he nodded and gave her the marble again. She poured, scraped, watched. This time she was not thinking about the grade she needed or the major she'd declared. She was thinking about the string in her grandmother's kitchen, the first crystal, the copied shape, the way the whole bowl learns from a few small pieces of what came before. The chocolate on the slab began to gather itself under her scraper. She pressed a smear to her lip, checked the coolness, and folded it back in. Mr. Bui looked over her shoulder and said, "Now pour."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
story:
The data table in Violet's lab manual had been photocopied so many times that the numbers looked faintly underwater. She traced a finger down the column for the reaction between nitrogen and hydrogen, watching the equilibrium constant shrink as the temperature climbed. At 400 degrees it stood tall; by 700 it had nearly folded in half. She had expected the opposite. Heat was energy, energy sped things up, so the constant should grow. Instead it fell, quietly, row by row, like a tide going out.

"You're frowning at paper again," Soren said, dropping onto the stool beside her. He wanted the period done with, wanted to be first out the door to the parking lot where the debate team was loading vans for regionals, but he had promised Mr. Hoffmann he would finish his table too. He reached over and tapped her page. "Mine does the same thing. I thought I copied it wrong."

Violet remembered the summer her grandmother tried to teach her chess, the old woman inculcating the rules through repetition until Violet could move the pieces in her sleep. Move a piece, she'd said, and the whole board answers. Violet had hated it then, the way nothing you did happened alone. Now she looked at the falling numbers and felt the same shiver of something rearranging itself in response.

Mr. Hoffmann moved between the benches, hands clasped behind his back, saying nothing. He never told them answers; he had once told the class, on the first day, that a teacher who explains everything is just an ideologue of explanation. Violet had written that down without understanding it. She thought she understood it a little now.

She flipped to the back of the manual, where a second table listed a different reaction, one marked endothermic. She ran her finger down the column and there it was, reversed: the constant rose as the temperature rose. She looked between the two tables, back and forth, like checking a translation.

"Soren," she said. "Yours is exothermic, right? The one you're doing." He nodded, half packing his bag. "Watch." She turned his manual toward him and pointed. "The K values fall when the temperature goes up. Mine falls too. But this one, the endothermic one, the K goes up with temperature. It's like they're opposites."

Soren leaned in despite himself, bag forgotten on his lap. "So heat hurts one and helps the other?"

"That's what the numbers say." She paused, because she was not entirely sure what the numbers were saying, only that they said it consistently. "Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant. Raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant. I don't know why yet. Maybe that's next week."

"You're willing to not know something? Voluntarily?" He grinned, but he copied the two tables side by side onto a fresh page before slinging his bag over his shoulder.

That night, before the debate van left, Soren texted her a photograph of his notebook with the caption: check the last row, I might have transposed two digits, tell me before Hoffmann sees it. Violet, cross-legged on her bed with a flashlight and the manual, checked. He had transposed them. She texted back: you did, fixed it for you, you owe me your third argument at regionals. Then she sat for a while longer, looking at the pattern, wondering whether the reaction itself could feel the heat arriving, whether it pushed back the way her grandmother's board pushed back, whether push was even the right word for something no one could watch happening.

The next morning the lab smelled of the janitor's soap and the windows were still dark. Mr. Hoffmann was writing the day's aim on the board. Violet raised her hand before the bell. "Yesterday, the tables. The K went down for the exothermic one when it got hotter, and up for the endothermic. Is that always true, or only for the ones in the book?"

He set the marker down. "What do your tables say?"

"They all agree. But four tables isn't everything."

"No," he said, and she could see the incipient smile he was trying to hold off, the kind he got when a question landed where he wanted it. "It isn't. Ask it again when you have forty."

She opened her notebook to a clean page and wrote, at the top, forty.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Biotech billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for $500 million, plus the assumption of pension obligations.
story:
The printer at the public library took ninety seconds a page, and Owen had eleven pages. He fed it quarters and watched the debate brief come out warm, one paragraph at a time, while behind him Hailee argued with the microfilm machine.

"You're loading it upside down," he said.

"I'm loading it the way the diagram shows."

"The diagram's from 1987."

The topic had been assigned Friday: whether a billionaire buying a newspaper counts as saving it or owning it. Owen had drawn the side he hadn't wanted, the side that said saving, and he'd spent the weekend looking for anything that would make him believe his own argument. Mr. Khoury, who judged the practice debates, had a habit of asking one quiet question at the end and watching you fold if your case was borrowed instead of built. Last month he'd asked Owen, "Do you believe that?" and Owen had said yes too quickly, and it had cost him the round.

Yosef arrived at four with a binder and a bag of chips he wasn't supposed to have in the building. He dropped into the chair across from Owen and read the top page upside down.

"So you're defending the rich guy," Yosef said.

"I'm defending one rich guy, once."

"Same thing."

"It's not." Owen turned the page around so Yosef could see the numbers he'd highlighted. "Patrick Soon-Shiong bought the Los Angeles Times in 2018 for five hundred million dollars. Plus he took on the pension obligations. That's the retirement money of everyone who works there."

Hailee abandoned the microfilm and came to look. "My uncle has a pension. He says the company holding it can just decide things about it."

"Then he should like this part," Owen said. "The buyer took those on. That's the whole case. A dying paper, and somebody with actual money decided it was worth half a billion plus the promises."

Yosef tore the corner off the chip bag with his teeth. "My cousin says the same guy can also decide what the paper says."

"Your cousin says a lot."

"He was there when they had layoffs."

Owen pulled the printouts toward himself and squared them. He had two piles now, though he hadn't admitted that to anyone. The left pile was the rescue: circulation was collapsing everywhere, papers were closing, and here was a surgeon who'd made a fortune in biotech stepping in with money nobody else would spend. The right pile was thinner but heavier. Editors who left. A story that got written and never ran. He didn't have proof of why the story died, and he knew the absence of proof wasn't proof of the opposite, but the not knowing sat in his stomach like a stone.

In the fall, for an English unit nobody had enjoyed, they'd sutured two essays together, cutting the seams of each and stitching the strongest parts into one paper, and Mr. Khoury had praised the result without saying it was easy. It hadn't been. The two essays argued against each other. Owen had solved it then with a paragraph beginning "Although" and a transition he was half proud of. This was different, because this time he had to hold both views in his own head at once, and there was no third position hiding under the desk. Either ownership was rescue or it was control, or it was both in amounts nobody could measure, and the measuring was exactly what the assignment refused to let him do.

"Look up 'existentialism,'" Hailee said suddenly, reading over his shoulder at his scrawled margin note. "Wait, why did you write that?"

"Because I couldn't sleep last night. There's a thing where you have to choose without knowing if the choice is right, and choosing is the whole point anyway. I think that's what I'm doing Tuesday."

"That's the worst use of philosophy I've ever heard," Yosef said, but he said it while pulling out his phone, so Owen knew he was going to look it up too.

Hailee went back to the microfilm and, on the third attempt, got it right. The screen glowed with an old front page, the whole broadsheet laid out like an alluvial fan, everything the city cared about that day spread out from the top headline downward, depositing sports and weather and opinion along the edges. She called them over. "This is the paper from before. Before the sale, I mean. Same name on top."

Owen stood between the screen and his two piles of paper. On the left, a man spending five hundred million dollars plus the pensions. On the right, a man who could spend five hundred million dollars and therefore decide things. The name on the front page hadn't changed. He tried the sentence out loud, quietly, in the half-empty reference room: "He saved it, and that's how he got it."

Yosef looked up from his phone. "That's actually not bad."

"It's not a conclusion, though."

"It's not supposed to be one. You have three minutes up there."

Owen sat back down, took out a pen, and drew a line down the center of a fresh page. On the left he wrote the purchase, the year, the amount, the pensions. On the right he wrote a single question mark, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. The printer was still chewing through page ten.

"Last quarter," he said, feeding the machine another coin.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The guitar had belonged to her grandfather, and it smelled like the inside of his car, which was to say like wintergreen mints and faintly like pipe smoke, though nobody in the family had smoked for eleven years. Sara carried it into Ms. Reyes's studio on the first Tuesday of September, holding it the way you hold something you're afraid of dropping, which is to say badly, with both arms and an elbow.

"He left it to me in the will," she said. "Along with a fondue set and forty years of National Geographic."

Ms. Reyes, who kept her studio above a dry cleaner and could name every student's worst habit within three lessons, took the guitar and turned it under the lamp. "When did anyone last tune it?"

"He died in March. So, March? Or possibly the nineties."

The strings, when Ms. Reyes plucked them, made sounds like a fence complaining. She handed Sara a small clip-on tuner and said only, "You'll want to learn this yourself. It's yours now." Then she went to make tea in the back room, which Sara understood was not rudeness but a policy: some things you find out alone.

Sara clipped the tuner to the headstock, where Dominik had shown her at the bus stop last week, and watched the little screen wake up green. She plucked the fattest string, the one closest to her face, and the screen flickered and settled on a letter. D. She turned the peg a little, then a little more, and the letter climbed and climbed and finally blinked E. So that was the lowest one, E. The next string wanted A, and after it D again, then G, then one that surprised her, B, and then, when she plucked the thinnest string, the screen said E, and Sara laughed out loud at the sheer nerve of it, the same letter coming back around like a bird returning to its branch. She wrote them on her wrist in pen, low to high: E A D G B E.

Last spring, before any of this, she had sat on her grandfather's porch step while he told a story about a pelagic fishing trip, forty miles out, where the ocean stopped being a place and became a condition, and he'd said the water out there was so deep a blue it transfigured the whole idea of color. She had been seventeen and restless and mostly waiting for her phone to charge. He had died before she thought to ask him to play.

Ms. Reyes came back with two mugs and watched Sara pluck the strings in order, listening. "Good," she said. "Now play a chord. Any chord. G is friendly."

G was not friendly. G was a small plebiscite in which four of Sara's fingers voted against the plan and the thumb abstained. The sound that came out was neither music nor its opposite but something in between, a sound with an argument inside it.

"Again," said Ms. Reyes.

Sara tried again. In the fourth or fifth attempt, something happened that she could not have described to Alexandre later, though she tried at lunch the next day, waving her hands: the chord stopped being six separate strings agreeing to be near each other and became one sound, whole and round, and it filled the little room above the dry cleaner and then it was gone, and she spent the rest of the lesson chasing it like a wave she'd already missed.

"I got it once," she told Alexandre, who was eating fries with the patience of a geologist.

"Once is once," he said. "Dominik got his license once and then hit a mailbox."

"That's not the same thing."

"It's exactly the same thing."

By October she could play four chords and change between three of them without stopping to look, and she had learned the names of the strings so thoroughly that she caught herself reciting them in the shower, E A D G B E, like a spell or a grocery list. Her grandfather, she was discovering, had loved this exact thing: the small, repeatable ritual of tuning, winding each string up to its letter, hearing the instrument come back to itself. She knew this now from a cassette his sister had mailed her, unlabeled, his voice on it saying, "Check the tuning first, always, before anything else," to someone who laughed, a woman, probably her grandmother, probably young.

The cost was harder to name than the gain. Every hour in the studio was an hour she wasn't at the lake with Dominik and Alexandre, who had stopped asking and started simply sending photos, the three of them a group photo that now had two people in it. And the gain itself refused to stay still. The chord that had come whole in September came rarely now, and when it did, it didn't mean what she'd thought it meant, closeness to him or to anything. It meant only that her hands had done something right for two seconds. She could not decide whether that was a small thing or the entire point, and Ms. Reyes, asked directly, had said only, "You're asking the wrong question," and refused to elaborate, which Sara found both infuriating and, privately, correct.

On the last Tuesday before the winter recital, Sara tuned the guitar herself, all six strings, low to high, without the tuner, listening instead of looking, and Ms. Reyes said nothing, which was her highest compliment. Then Sara set her fingers on a G chord, breathed, and began.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
story:
Arianna had the kitchen to herself until six, which gave her exactly two hours to learn what four YouTube videos had so far failed to teach her: how to make chocolate set with a shine and a snap instead of the dull, fingerprinted slabs she kept producing. The counter was already strewn with evidence of failure, bits of failed bark in a bowl she was too stubborn to throw out. She chopped a bar of dark chocolate into even pieces, set the double boiler over barely simmering water, and told herself that this time she would actually pay attention to the thermometer instead of trusting her nerve.

Alexy arrived at four with a plastic bag and an apology already half formed. "I left these in the car yesterday," he said, tipping a box of truffles onto the counter. Every one of them wore greyish streaks across the top, white and dull, like frost that had decided to stay. "It was warm, like really warm, and they were a gift for Jean's thing. Are they ruined?"

Arianna picked one up and turned it under the window light. The streaks caught nothing, gave back nothing, just a flat film where shine should have been. She had seen this before, on her own failures, but hers had come out of the fridge, not a car. She set the truffle down carefully, the way you set down something that might be evidence. "They're not moldy," she said. "I know that much. I've been reading about this all week, actually. There's a name for it. Fat bloom."

"Sounds malevolent," Alexy said, and she laughed even though she didn't want to, because he was right, the phrase had that quality, like something out of a Victorian pamphlet on household dangers. "It's a dull grey or white streaky film that shows up on chocolate that wasn't tempered properly, or that melted and reset. It's still okay to eat, probably." She heard the hedge in her own voice and hated it. The book had been clear. The car's heat had melted the truffles and they had reset badly, and that was all anyone could say for certain.

"So fix them," Alexy said. He had the talent of making things sound like small favors when they were not. "You're the one doing the chocolate project. Jean's thing is at seven."

She wanted to tell him that tempering was the whole project precisely because it kept defeating her, that the melted truffles would have to be remade from scratch, that melting and resetting badly was exactly how you got more bloom, not less. Instead she cogitated for a moment, turning the problem over the way she turned the truffle, and found that the two troubles might be the same trouble. Her slabs failed because she hadn't controlled the cooling. His truffles had failed because the car had melted them and they reset wrong. If she could learn to coax chocolate into setting correctly, she could rescue his gift and prove something to herself at the same time. If she couldn't, she would fail in front of a witness, which was worse.

"Get me the baking bar from the pantry," she said. "And don't touch anything."

She melted two-thirds of the chopped chocolate to forty-five degrees, pulled the bowl off the heat, and stirred in the remaining third, watching the thermometer slide down through the thirties. Alexy read numbers aloud for her while she stirred in slow figure eights, because the book said agitation mattered as much as temperature, and she was beginning to believe it. At thirty-one degrees the chocolate ribboned off the spatula in a thick, glossy rope. She dipped the back of a spoon, set it on parchment, and put it in the cool pantry rather than the fridge, because the fridge had betrayed her before with condensation.

They waited, which was its own kind of work. Alexy told a story about Mr. Dlamini calling him a revisionist historian for arguing that the textbook had the sequence of events backwards, and Arianna half listened, checking the pantry every few minutes like a person who knows checking doesn't speed anything up. When she brought the spoon out, the chocolate had set firm. She held it under the light. It shone. She snapped it against the counter and it broke with a clean, hard click, the sound she had heard only in videos until now.

The remaking of the truffles was slower and uglier. She melted the bloomed ones down, which felt like destroying the gift a second time, and re-tempered in smaller batches, and two batches went grey on her anyway before she got the hang of holding the temperature steady. By six-thirty there were nine rescued truffles, unevenly dipped, one with her thumbprint pressed into its base where she had grabbed it too soon. She boxed them in paper and set the lid on crooked. "It's not what they were," she said. "Tell Jean that honestly, or don't. Your call."

Alexy took the box and turned it over in his hands, studying the one visible truffle through the cellophane window, the shine she had given it, the seam along its base where her dipping had been clumsy. "It's better," he said. "It's just also worse than the original in a way I can't describe."

"Then describe it to her like that," Arianna said, and scraped the last of the tempered chocolate from the bowl onto a spoon, holding it up to watch the light sit on it, perfectly, for exactly as long as it took to fall.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election.
story:
The debate was in the city hall chamber at four o'clock, and by three Clara was still sitting on the front steps with her notes face down on her knees, because looking at them made her feel worse. Eleni had claimed the presidential side weeks ago, back when the assignment seemed abstract, and Clara had been left defending the parliamentary system, which until Monday she had assumed was just the British word for Congress.

"You could still flip a coin," Eleni said, dropping onto the step beside her with a bottle of orange juice and no sympathy. "Bethany said nobody in the audience would know the difference anyway."

"That's the problem. Mr. Pelletier will know the difference." Mr. Pelletier taught the civics elective and had volunteered the chamber, the podium, and an audience of parents and off-duty council members, presumably for his own amusement. He had also told them, on Monday, that he would be listening for substance rather than volume, which everyone understood to mean volume.

Inside, the chamber smelled of floor wax and photocopier toner. Bethany was already arranging chairs with the grim efficiency of someone who had done this before. "Fixed terms are simpler," she said, not looking up. "You vote for a president, the president serves four years, that's it. Even my little brother gets it."

"Simple isn't the same as good," Clara said, and then, because she had nothing to follow it with, went to find the water fountain.

What she actually had was a library book with a cracked spine, checked out Tuesday and annotated in three colors, and a fact she had found at eleven the night before that she kept turning over like a coin with two different faces. On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election. One vote. She had read the sentence four times and then looked up the date to make sure it wasn't a typo, and then read it again. Her mother liked to say that one vote never changed anything, usually in the tone she reserved for weather.

The trouble was that the same fact cut both ways, and Clara could feel both edges. In a parliamentary system, the legislature could pull the cord and stop the whole government between elections; in a presidential one, the head of government served a fixed term no matter how badly things went, unless you reached for impeachment, which was slow, rare, and in her book described with a vocabulary that ran to words like chicanery. The parliamentary version put power nearer to the votes. The presidential version made you wait, but it also made you safe from a government falling apart every time a majority got nervous.

At four o'clock the chamber filled. A councilwoman in the second row. Parents. Mr. Pelletier by the wall with a clipboard, which was a noxious development, in Clara's opinion, since clipboards implied grading and grading implied that the clipboard had always been there, waiting.

Eleni opened smoothly. She talked about stability and separation of powers, and she was good, and Clara watched the councilwoman nod along and thought about valorizing a system, the way people did, treating a constitution like a moral achievement rather than a machine with particular bolts in particular places. When her turn came she stood at the podium, took a breath, and told the room about 28 March 1979. She said the numbers slowly. "Three hundred eleven to three hundred ten. The government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, and there had to be a general election." She let it sit for a second. "In a parliamentary system, one vote in the chamber can do that. In a presidential system, nothing like it can happen. You wait for the term to end."

"Or you impeach," Eleni said from her seat.

"How often?" Clara asked, and Eleni didn't answer, because they both knew.

Afterward, the councilwoman asked a question about whether letting a majority topple a government was just a faster road to chaos. Clara said she genuinely didn't know. She said the presidential system guarded against a bad week, and the parliamentary system guarded against a bad four years, and she had not yet worked out which guard she trusted more. Mr. Pelletier wrote something on the clipboard. Bethany, stacking chairs, mouthed "nice" at her across the room.

Outside, the evening had gone cool, and Eleni caught up with her on the steps with the orange juice, mostly empty now, rolling in her hand. "You really believe the one vote thing decides it?"

"No," Clara said. "It doesn't decide anything. It just means my mother's wrong, and that's worth knowing for its own sake."

Eleni held out the bottle. "There's a swallow left."

Clara took it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
The parking lot had filled with cars by the time Sofia found her cap, which had blown under a minivan and sat there like a discarded frisbee. She bent to retrieve it, and when she straightened, Abram was leaning against the chain-link fence with his hands in his pockets, the way he had leaned against things since seventh grade.

"You look official," he said, nodding at the cap. He gesticulated vaguely at her gown, at the tassel, at the whole ceremony of it, as though he were presenting a game show prize. He had not walked across any stage. He'd left school in October of their junior year, and this was the first time since then that Sofia had seen him outside the gas station where he applied, unsuccessfully, for work.

"I feel like a magician's assistant," she said. Behind them, Mr. Qureshi was trying to organize the leftover programs into stacks, a project that everyone knew would end with the wind doing whatever it wanted.

They stood a while in the smell of asphalt and someone's exhaust. Then Abram said, without preamble, "Thirty-one applications. You know how many called back? Two. One was a scam."

Sofia had been composing a congratulatory remark about her own day, and now she let it dissolve. "What does Louka's dad say? Doesn't he know people at the warehouse?"

"Louka's dad says a lot." Abram picked at the fence. "Louka says more."

Louka arrived then, still in his gown with the collar of his shirt sticking out at the neck, carrying two popsicles from the ice cream truck that always materialized near large gatherings of teenagers, like a shark sensing something. He handed one to Abram without comment, which Sofia understood to be the whole point of Louka.

"I was telling her about the applications," Abram said.

"I looked it up," Louka said, because Louka looked everything up, including once the etymology of Sofia's name at her own birthday party. "For last year, 2023. If you're twenty-five or older and you've got a high school diploma, unemployment was 3.9 percent. No diploma, 5.6 percent." He said it the way he recited etymologies, flat and precise, and then he looked at the popsicle as if it had betrayed him.

Abram was quiet. Sofia watched him do the arithmetic in his face, the small adjustment of a man discovering that his bad luck was also a statistic. "So there's a number now," he said finally. "That's comforting. I'm not failing individually. I'm failing at scale."

"It's 2023," Louka said. "You're not even twenty-five."

"Great. I have three years to become a rounding error."

In October of junior year, Sofia remembered, Abram had announced his departure from school with the confidence of someone reading a maxim off a pillow: less talk, more money. He had a plan involving his cousin's landscaping business in another state, and Sofia had believed him because he said it in the cafeteria with a burrito in his hand, and people holding burritos are rarely lying. The cousin's business, it turned out, had a cousin of its own, and the plan dissolved somewhere over the winter without either of them ever discussing it. What they had discussed, once, on the bleachers, was whether it mattered, a conversation in which Sofia had said something about doors closing and Abram had said doors were for people who could afford houses. She had thought that was very funny at the time. She thought about it now and laughed less.

Mr. Qureshi came over, still holding his defeated stack of programs. "Sofia. You're the one who wrote about the port cities, yes? The essay." He had taught them geography for one semester and had called the trade routes of the fifteenth century cosmopolitan, a word Sofia had stolen immediately and never returned. "Very good work. What are you doing next?"

"College," she said. "In the fall. Supposedly." She heard the supposedly and disliked it, but it had escaped.

"You'll go far," Mr. Qureshi said, and then, because he was incapable of leaving a parking lot without tidying it, he drifted off toward an abandoned folding chair.

Sofia turned the popsicle stick over in her fingers. She wanted to say something to Abram that was true and useful, and she could not find a single sentence that was both. The numbers said school mattered; she believed the numbers; and yet here was Abram, who was sharper than half the people crossing the stage today, holding a popsicle next to a fence. Maybe the numbers measured something other than the thing she wanted them to measure. Maybe both were true and she would have to carry them together, the way you carry two bags when one is awkward.

"One of the call-backs," Abram said, "was the hardware store. The guy said come back after the summer. He hires everyone after the summer."

"That's something," Sofia said.

"It's a maybe. I've got a collection of maybes." But he said it lightly, and he was smiling a little, and Louka was already trying to balance his popsicle stick on the fence post, so it could not be entirely hopeless.

"You'll come to the thing at Louka's," Sofia said. "Tonight. There's a pool."

"There's an above-ground pool," Louka said, as if correcting the record.

Abram peeled the last of the wrapper off his popsicle. "I'll come," he said. "I'm not swimming in that tub."

He flicked the wrapper toward the trash can by the fence. It caught the edge, spun, and dropped in, and all three of them watched it as though it meant something.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
Maelie dragged the whiteboard out of the garage and propped it against the fence, its corner sinking into the grass where the sprinklers had missed. On it she had written the week: Monday sprints, Tuesday sprints, Wednesday sprints, with a question mark after Thursday. Mederick lay on the picnic blanket with a bag of frozen peas pressed to his calves, groaning theatrically every time a cloud moved.

"I can't feel my legs," he announced. "Travis, tell her."

Travis was doing his best to look neutral, which for Travis meant chewing a toothpick and squinting at the whiteboard like it owed him money. "We did feel fine, though," he said. "Monday night I felt great. I walked home. I ate two sandwiches."

Maelie tapped the marker against her teeth. That was the part that had bothered her too. Monday's session had been the hardest thing any of them had done, and they had all walked out of the yard laughing, trading plans for the season. Then Wednesday morning Mederick had texted her a photo of himself gripping the kitchen counter captioned "help," and by Wednesday evening Travis had taken the stairs at school on his hands and knees, or so he claimed, and Mederick had missed practice entirely. She had felt it too, a deep ache in her thighs that arrived like a bill for something she'd already forgotten buying.

"Wednesday," she said slowly, drawing a circle around the day on the board. "We did the work Monday. We felt fine Monday. Wednesday we couldn't walk."

"Delayed-onset muscle soreness," said Mederick, with the air of a man delivering a diagnosis. He had looked it up at two in the morning, unable to sleep because turning over in bed hurt. "It peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours after a hard or unfamiliar workout. Not right after. So it was coming for us the whole time. We just didn't know it yet."

"Two days of feeling like heroes," Travis said, "and then the invoice."

Mr. Ortiz, who had been watering his tomatoes on the other side of the fence, leaned over it now, because Mr. Ortiz leaned over the fence the way other people checked their mail. In his day, he said, the coach would run them until they dropped and call it character. He said it without gravitas, almost apologetically, the way you admit to having once believed something embarrassing. He had liked it at the time, he said. He had also, at fifty-eight, both knees wrapped like parcels, begun to suspect the coach had been an obstreperous old man who mistaken cruelty for curriculum. He did not tell her what to do. He watered his tomatoes, shook his head at his younger self, and went back inside.

Maelie stood at the whiteboard for a long time. Her old plan rested on one idea, that more work meant more progress, and it sat there now looking thin. But Mederick's opposite idea, that soreness meant injury and she should indemnify them all against effort by padding the week with rest, seemed just as flimsy; he wanted a contract that protected them from the sport itself. She erased Thursday's question mark and wrote REST in big letters. Under Monday she wrote WARM-UP, 15 MIN, EASY. Then she spread the hard days apart, hard Monday, easy Tuesday, hard Thursday, easy Friday, and put a long rest where Wednesday used to be, the day the soreness would come to collect whether they planned for it or not.

"Will it still hurt?" Travis asked, studying the board. "Thursday's session. After the rest day."

She wanted to say no. She was pretty sure the answer was still some version of yes, that soreness would keep arriving on its own schedule for a while, that she was guessing at distances she couldn't measure yet. "Probably," she said. "But we'll be able to walk while it does. That's the version one."

Mederick peeled the bag of peas off his calves, stood, took two experimental steps, and winced with what she chose to read as approval. "Version one," he said, and limped over to stand beside her at the board, where the week now had gaps in it on purpose, gaps that looked, from the fence, almost like breathing.
